Even for a man known capable of the greatest discoveries, all that others could do would be to defray the expense of his experiments and protect his leisure from interruption.
I neither promise anything extraordinary, nor imagine the public much interested in my designs, nor have a soul so mean as to accept a favour I might be thought unworthy of.
Publishing my physics would not bring me any help with experiments that I could usefully accept.

meta.note: Not stated in so many words; it is the upshot of VI.7 and one of the considerations VI.8 says were taken together.

statements.text: I should publish this discourse together with some particular specimens of my philosophy, giving the public an account of my doings and designs.

meta.note: The specimens are the essays published with the Discourse (the Dioptrics and Meteorics are named in VI.10). This reconciles the case for communicating findings with withholding the physics.

statements.text: If I published nothing, many who knew of my earlier intention to publish might imagine my reasons for refraining were less to my credit than they really are.
I am not immoderately desirous of glory, and am even averse to it insofar as it is hostile to repose, which I value above everything else.

meta.note: VI.12 adds that he will be more obliged to those who let him enjoy his retirement undisturbed than to any who offer the highest preferments.

statements.text: I have never sought to hide my actions as if they were crimes, since such concealment would wrong me and would disturb the tranquillity I seek.
Though indifferent alike to fame and to being forgotten, I have been unable to prevent myself from acquiring some sort of reputation.
I am bound to do my best at least to save myself from being ill spoken of.
My design of self-instruction suffers daily more delay for want of the countless experiments I need, which I cannot make without the assistance of others.
I owe it to myself not to give posterity ground to reproach me that things could have been left far more perfect had I made known how they might have helped.
I can select matters that provoke little controversy and expound no more of my principles than I wish, yet show clearly what I can and cannot accomplish in the sciences.
Readers who see an objection and my reply together will more easily determine where the truth lies.
Those who have objections to my writings should send them to my publisher, so that I may append my reply.

meta.note: He undertakes to avow errors frankly when convinced of them, or else briefly to state his defence, adding no new matter.

statements.text: In the Dioptrics and Meteorics the last matters are demonstrated by the first, which are their causes, and the first in turn by the last, which are their effects.
Experience renders the majority of these effects most certain.
The causes I deduce these effects from serve not to establish their reality but to explain their existence, while the reality of the causes is established by the reality of the effects.
My reasoning from causes to effects and from effects to causes is not the fallacy that logicians call a circle.
I call my starting points hypotheses only to signal that I believe I can deduce them from the first truths I have expounded, though I have expressly determined not to do so.
Some minds, thinking to master in a day what took another twenty years, would build extravagant philosophies on what they took to be my principles, and I would be blamed for it.
I should not, in these essays, deduce my hypotheses from my first principles.
If their reasons are well considered, my opinions will be found so simple and so conformed to common sense as to appear less extraordinary than any others on the same subjects.
I have adopted my opinions neither because others held them nor because they did not, but solely because reason has convinced me of their truth.

meta.note: Part VI's restatement of the first precept of method (II.7) as a description of his practice.

statements.text: Making and adjusting the machines I describe without overlooking the smallest detail requires skill and practice; success at the first attempt would be as astonishing as mastering the guitar in a day.
No one is entitled to condemn the invention explained in the Dioptrics because artisans cannot execute it at once.
Those who use their unprejudiced natural reason will be better judges of my opinions than those who heed only the writings of the ancients.
Those who unite good sense with study, whom alone I desire as judges, will not be so partial to Latin as to refuse my reasoning because it is in the vulgar tongue.
Writing in French reaches readers who use their natural reason but do not read Latin.

meta.note: Implicit: the choice of French only serves the stated purpose if the readers he wants as judges are reachable in French and not in Latin.

statements.text: I should write in French, the language of my country, rather than in Latin, the language of my teachers.
I should not bind myself to the public by any promise about my future progress that I am not certain of being able to fulfil.
My inclination is so opposed to all other pursuits, especially those that cannot help some without harming others, that I could not succeed in them if constrained to engage in them.

arguments.justification: Everyone is content with his share of good sense, and it is not likely that all are mistaken in this; so the conviction testifies that the power of judging rightly, which is what good sense means, is by nature equal in all.

Since reason is equal in all, unequal reason cannot explain why we disagree; and since what matters is applying the mind rightly, the difference must lie in the paths along which we conduct our thoughts and the objects we attend to.

The greatest minds fall into the greatest errors, and the slow traveller on the straight road outstrips the runner who leaves it; so capacity by itself secures nothing and right application is what counts.

Reason is what constitutes us as men, so it belongs to our form or nature; and difference of degree holds only among accidents, not among the forms of individuals of one species; hence reason is found complete in each individual.

meta.note: A second, independent argument for the same conclusion, adopted from 'the common opinion of philosophers'.

arguments.justification: The fruits I have already reaped from the method are such that I cannot help expecting the same of the future; what has increased my knowledge so far will go on increasing it.

Almost every human pursuit appears vain and useless, whereas my own search for truth has given me real progress and the highest satisfaction; so if any occupation is excellent and important, it is this one.

The fruits I claim to have reaped from my method are these: truths of some importance discovered daily, of which other men are generally ignorant, and a satisfaction more perfect than any other I know; hence the highest satisfaction in the progress I believe I have made in the search for truth.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. The fruits announced in I.3 are described in III.5.

arguments.justification: Since we are so liable to deceive ourselves in what concerns us, my satisfaction with my own progress may itself be a delusion: copper and glass taken for gold and diamonds.

Because I may be deceived about myself and cannot trust the favourable judgments of friends, laying my course open for each reader to judge gives me, in the general opinion, a further aid to instruction that I would otherwise lack.

To give precepts is to claim greater skill than one's readers and to invite censure for the slightest error; I make no such claim for my mind, so I offer only a history of how I have conducted my own reason.
If I was not judged inferior to my fellows, some of whom were destined to become teachers, and our age is as rich in able minds as any, then my own case is a fair sample by which to judge others.

I was promised clear and certain knowledge from letters; yet after the complete course at one of the best schools in Europe, and all the extra reading I could find, I was left with only doubts and the discovery of my ignorance. If I may judge others by myself, no one has found such a science, so it does not exist.

Each branch of the schools' studies has some genuine use or beauty, and even the most error-ridden repay some attention so that their worth can be judged; so, despite my disillusion, the studies as a whole still deserve esteem.

A narrative that admits impossible events, or that omits the mean and ordinary circumstances, does not represent life as it is; those who model their conduct on it therefore attempt projects beyond their powers, like the knights-errant of romance.

Reading the ancients is a kind of travel: a little of it corrects our judgment of our own customs, but too much makes us strangers to our own time; and fables and histories additionally mislead those who take them as models. So the time I had already given them was sufficient.

The best persuaders are those with the strongest reason, even without rhetoric, and the best poets those with the richest fancy, even without the art of poetry; so both excellences come from nature rather than from study.

Reasonings that are certain and evident make a foundation strong and solid; yet if all mathematics yields is the mechanical arts, nothing lofty has been raised on that foundation, which is what astonished me.

The ancients praise virtue magnificently but supply no criterion for it, so their fine names may cover apathy, pride, or worse; a magnificent structure with no secure foundation is a palace built on sand.

The revealed truths surpass our comprehension, and heaven is as open to the ignorant as to the learned; so my reason is neither competent to examine them nor needed for salvation, and examining them would require more than human help.
Every matter in philosophy is still disputed, and what the learned still dispute is not above doubt; therefore nothing in philosophy is above doubt.
The most distinguished minds have worked at philosophy for ages and settled nothing beyond doubt; my mind is no better than theirs; so I cannot expect to succeed where they have not.

Where learned men uphold many conflicting opinions on one matter and only one can be true, any particular opinion is far more likely false than true; so what is merely probable should be counted as well-nigh false.

The other sciences take their principles from philosophy, and nothing in philosophy is above doubt; since nothing solid can rest on uncertain foundations, no solid superstructure can be raised in them.

Having read even the most curious and rare books, and holding that some attention to every study is what lets us judge its worth and avoid deception, I had learned enough of the false sciences to see through their professors.

meta.note: Reconstructed link: Descartes states the premise (I.7) and the conclusion (I.13) but does not spell out the inference.

arguments.justification: I had no need to sell science to make my fortune, and I cared little for honor obtained through fictitious titles; so neither the riches nor the honors the sciences promise could move me to cultivate them.

For all these reasons together: letters yielded no certain science; I had read enough of the ancients; eloquence and poetry cannot be learned; mathematics, though certain, had nothing lofty built on it; the ancient morals rest on sand; theology is beyond reason; philosophy offers nothing beyond dispute and the merely probable is nearly false; the other sciences inherit philosophy's infirmity and their rewards do not tempt me; and the false sciences hold no more for me. Nothing remained to seek in books, so I turned to myself and to the world.

A man reasoning about his own affairs is soon punished by events if he judges badly, whereas a scholar's speculations carry no consequences and only reward vanity the further they stray from common sense; so the former holds far more truth.

Having resolved to seek knowledge only in myself or in the world, and wanting to learn to tell true from false, I should go where the truer reasoning is found: among men engaged in affairs that concern them, in courts and armies and every condition of life.

If great nations approve by common consent what seems absurd to us, and men's manners contradict one another as much as the philosophers do, then what our own custom approves may be equally absurd; persuasion by example and custom is therefore no ground for firm belief.
By withholding firm belief from whatever custom alone had persuaded me of, I gradually shed the custom-based errors that darken our natural light and keep us from listening to reason.

Having given up books for either myself or the world, and having found in several years of studying the world no more settled conviction than in books, the remaining place to seek the truth I desired was myself; so I resolved to make myself my object of study and to use all my mind's powers in choosing my path.
Because my years abroad had first rid me of many errors that darken the intelligence, the study of myself that followed succeeded better than it could have had I never left my country or my books.
Buildings and cities show the same pattern: what one hand plans freely comes out better than what many hands patch together over time. I take this to hold of works generally.

In the same way as with buildings and cities, laws determined piecemeal by many, under the pressure of particular crimes and disputes, will be less perfect than the appointments of a single wise legislator followed from the start.
The ordinances of the true religion come from God alone, a single and perfect author; so by the same principle its constitution must be incomparably superior to every merely human one.

meta.note: Descartes writes 'it is thus quite certain', presenting it as an immediate application of the principle.

arguments.justification: Sparta's laws taken singly were often strange and even opposed to good morals, so its pre-eminence cannot be due to their individual goodness. What remains is that they came from one man and all tended to a single end, which the principle says makes for perfection.

The book sciences without demonstrations are the opinions of many different individuals massed together, a work of many hands. By the principle they must be farther from truth than the simple inferences one man of good sense, using his natural and unprejudiced judgment, draws from his own experience.

Our judgments were formed under many conflicting authorities, our desires and our preceptors, rather than by reason alone. Like any work of many hands they cannot be as solid as if one mature reason had guided us from birth.

As no one pulls down all the houses of a town merely to rebuild it more handsomely, so a private individual should not overturn a state, or the body of the sciences and the order of teaching in the schools, which are large bodies of the same kind, in order to set it up amended.

Large bodies once overthrown are hard to set up again and their fall is disastrous; the defects of states have been smoothed by custom and are more tolerable than the change needed to remove them; whereas the difficulties in reforming my own opinions have remedies. So even the slightest public reform is incomparably harder than my private one.

A private individual may, and when the foundations are insecure must, take down his own house to rebuild it. My opinions are my own house; their foundations, principles taken on trust and judgments formed under desires and preceptors, are insecure; and, unlike public reform, the difficulties are remediable. So I should sweep them wholly away and rebuild, and will conduct my life far better than by leaning on old foundations.

meta.note: Descartes: 'I firmly believed that in this way I should much better succeed in the conduct of my life, than if I built only upon old foundations.'

arguments.justification: Hence: since it is preposterous for a private individual to set about reforming the state, those called by neither birth nor fortune to public affairs should not be forever projecting reforms of them.

The majority of men fall into two classes: the precipitate, who would lose their way for life if they once doubted their accustomed opinions, and the modest, who ought rather to follow their betters. For neither class is the design of stripping away all beliefs fitting, so it should not be undertaken by everyone.

Philosophers have defended every absurdity; nations opposed to us reason as well as we do; the same mind would think differently if raised elsewhere; fashions reverse within a decade. The best account of this variety is that our opinions rest on custom and example rather than on any certain knowledge.

Deferring to one's betters, as the modest should, requires someone who judges better. But opinions rest on custom, which is no ground for firm belief; the majority is no guarantee of truth where truth is hard to find; and I could select no one whose opinions deserved preference. So there was no one to defer to, and I was constrained to use my own reason.

Having to rely on my own reason, and knowing that those who doubt hastily lose their way for life, I should go like a man walking alone in the dark: slowly and circumspectly, so that if I do not advance far I at least do not fall, and before dismissing any opinion first understand the task and find the true method.

Logic, geometrical analysis, and algebra were the three arts I expected to contribute to my design. But logic serves to communicate rather than to discover, and its good precepts are buried among bad; analysis fatigues the imagination and algebra confuses the mind. By these considerations I was induced to seek another method with the advantages of the three and none of their defects.

As a state is best governed by a few laws rigidly administered rather than a multitude that hampers justice, so, in place of logic's many mixed precepts, a few precepts unfailingly observed would be perfectly sufficient for the method I seek.

Needing a method with the advantages of the three arts and none of their defects, and believing four precepts sufficient if never once neglected, I adopted these four, together with the firm resolution never to fail in observing them.

meta.note: The four precepts and the resolution are asserted jointly: Descartes presents them as one method, and the sufficiency claim is conditional on the resolution.

arguments.justification: The geometers reach their hardest conclusions by long chains of simple, easy reasonings. This led me to imagine that everything man can know is connected in the same way, and so is reachable provided we accept nothing false as true and always keep the order needed to deduce one truth from another.

I was already persuaded that one must begin with the simplest and easiest objects; and since of all who have sought truth in the sciences only the mathematicians have found demonstrations, that must have been the rule of their investigations too. So I resolved to begin with the simplest objects, those of mathematics.

I did not intend to master every particular science called mathematics; but since, however different their objects, they all consider only the proportions among them, it is best for my purpose to study proportions in the most general form, so that I can afterwards apply them to every class of objects where they legitimately hold.

To understand proportions I must sometimes consider them one by one and sometimes hold many in mind at once. Straight lines are the simplest and most distinctly imaginable objects for the former, and the briefest symbols are best for the latter.

Lines give the concreteness of geometrical analysis without confining the understanding to figures that fatigue the imagination; brief symbols give the compactness of algebra without its obscuring rules and formulas. So each of the two arts corrects the other's defects.

The reasonings of mathematics are certain and evident, whereas in philosophy, and in the sciences that borrow their principles from it, nothing is above doubt; so of all who have sought truth in the sciences, the mathematicians alone have found demonstrations, that is, certain and evident reasons.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. II.11 states the observation; I.10 and I.12 supply the contrast it rests on.

arguments.justification: Because I began with the simplest and most general truths, in the order the third precept prescribes, each truth I discovered was available as a rule for finding the ones that followed.

The accurate observance of these few precepts, beginning with the simplest and most general truths so that each truth found became a rule for the next, is what gave me such ease that in two or three months I solved questions I had thought very hard and determined how far others could be solved.

meta.note: Descartes reports the success as a fact and says the results are 'attributable to' starting with the simplest truths; the argument records that attribution.

arguments.justification: Since the truth on any point is one, whoever apprehends it has all that can be known on that point; a child who has correctly added by rule can be assured he has found everything human genius can find about that sum.

What makes the child's arithmetic certain is that he follows the true order and exactly enumerates all the conditions of the sum. My third and fourth precepts prescribe just this, so my method includes all that gives certitude to the rules of arithmetic.

Since I had not restricted the method to any particular matter, and it had succeeded so well in the two mathematical sciences, and all knowable things are connected in the same way as the geometers' chains, I hoped to apply it to the other sciences with no less success.

To attack all the difficulties of the sciences at once would violate the order the method prescribes; and knowledge of the sciences depends on principles borrowed from philosophy, in which I found nothing certain. So I must first try to establish the principles of philosophy.

Establishing the principles of philosophy is the most important inquiry and the one where precipitancy is most to be dreaded; my first precept forbids precipitancy; and I was only twenty-three. So I should not approach it until more mature, and should first prepare by eradicating my errors, gathering experience, and practising my method.

Just as one who pulls down the house he lives in must have another to live in while rebuilding, so I, having resolved to demolish my opinions and suspend judgement, still had to act without delay, avoid irresolution and live as happily as I could; hence I needed a provisional morality to live by in the meantime.
Because action often cannot wait, suspending judgement must not become suspending action; I must not be irresolute in what I do.
Having resolved to subject all my opinions to examination, I could not meanwhile rely on any of them; for the interim I held them for nought.
Since my own opinions are set aside and I must nevertheless act, I could not do better than follow, for the time being, the opinions of the most judicious.
Even though people as judicious as ours may exist among the Persians and Chinese, expediency dictates that I regulate my practice by the opinions of those among whom I must live.
Since believing a thing and knowing that one believes it are different acts of mind, and the one is often found without the other, many people do not know what they really believe.

To learn the real opinions of the judicious I should look at what they do rather than what they say: few say exactly what they believe, and many do not even know what they believe, so their words are an unreliable guide.

The most moderate opinions are always the most convenient for practice and probably the best, since all excess is generally vicious; so among opinions of equal repute I should choose the most moderate.
If I err, a moderate choice leaves me nearer the truth than an extreme would if the opposite extreme turned out to be right; so I should choose the moderate opinion.

meta.note: An independent second reason for the same rule.

arguments.justification: Because nothing on earth is wholly beyond change, and because I hope to perfect my judgements rather than let them deteriorate, it would be a grave sin against good sense to bind myself to hold something good later merely because I approve of it now, when it may have ceased to be good or I to think it so.
Since binding my future judgement is a sin against good sense, I place all promises that abridge freedom among the extremes that my rule of moderation tells me to avoid.

The truths of faith have always held first place in my belief and are above the reach of my reason; they are therefore not among the opinions I set aside for examination, and I adhere firmly to the faith I was raised in.

meta.note: Interpretive link: Descartes reserves the truths of faith rather than arguing for them; the Part I statement supplies the reason he gives elsewhere for not examining them.

arguments.justification: Following the judicious people I live among, reading their real opinions in their practice, which includes their laws and customs, preferring the most moderate of those opinions, and keeping my faith, together make up my first maxim.
Since holding a steady course, even one chosen by chance, brings travellers at least to some place better than the middle of a forest, they ought to keep one direction rather than wander or stay put.

Since in action no delay is often permissible, when I cannot determine the truth I must act on the most probable; and where neither option is more probable I must still choose one rather than not act.
What determines my choice is that I must act and cannot wait; that necessity is itself certain and true even when the opinion chosen is not.

Having chosen a course on the most probable opinion, or on an arbitrary one where nothing favours either, I should treat the choice as certain in practice, because the reason for making it, that I must act, is itself certain and true.
In holding to adopted opinions as steadfastly as if they were certain, I imitate travellers lost in a forest who keep going one way rather than wander or stand still.
If I must act on the most probable, choose one course even where none is more probable, and then treat the choice as certain in practice, then I should be as firm and resolute in my actions as I can.

meta.note: Independent of the travellers analogy; the principled derivation.

arguments.justification: Remorse comes from vacillating between courses for want of a determinate principle of choice; a firm resolve to hold the adopted course removes the vacillation and so the remorse.
If nothing but our thoughts is absolutely in our power, then once we have done our best in external things whatever we still fail in was, as regards us, impossible.

Since the will seeks only what the understanding presents as attainable, if we regard all external goods as equally beyond our power we will no more regret their absence than we regret not owning the kingdoms of China, or not having wings; we make a virtue of necessity.
If regarding external goods as beyond my power removes regret and desire for them, then this single persuasion suffices to keep me from desiring what I cannot obtain, and hence to make me content.

The ancient philosophers' happiness amid poverty is best explained by their incessant meditation on the limits nature set to their power: convinced that only their thoughts were theirs, they ceased to desire other things and gained absolute command of their thoughts.
The philosophers who mastered their thoughts and desires in this way became happy; their example confirms that this persuasion suffices for contentment.

meta.note: Independent second support for the same conclusion.

arguments.justification: Those who command their thoughts can realise all their desires, whereas the favourites of fortune who lack this philosophy cannot; so the former have ground to think themselves richer, more powerful, freer and happier.

Since I should live as happily as I can, and accustoming myself to the persuasion that only my thoughts are in my power suffices for contentment, I should conquer myself rather than fortune and change my desires rather than the order of the world.

Reviewing the occupations of men, I could choose none better than the one I was already in, which I had long held to be the one truly excellent occupation of men as men: my method gives me the purest satisfaction I think possible in this life, and daily discoveries that leave me indifferent to everything else.

Since God has given each of us a light of reason for distinguishing truth from error, and since I had already found myself constrained to rely on my own reason rather than on the opinions of others, I could not think it right to rest for a moment on another's opinions unless I meant to examine them by my own judgement as soon as I was able.

The first maxim is tolerable only if I mean to examine others' opinions myself; the second only if following doubtful opinions forfeits no better ones; the third only if I am on a sure path to knowledge and the true good. So all three rest on the design of continuing to instruct myself.
Since my whole provisional morality presupposes that I continue the work of instructing myself, continuing that work is the occupation I should keep.

meta.note: Offered as an additional reason ('Besides, the three preceding maxims were founded singly on the design of continuing the work of self-instruction').

arguments.justification: Since we seek or shun things only as the understanding judges them good or bad, right judgement is all that is needed for right action, and the most correct judgement for the best action.

The most correct judgement produces the best action, which is the acquisition of all the virtues and all else truly valuable within our reach; and assurance of acquiring these cannot fail to make us content.
If the most correct judgement is the source of all virtue and of contentment, then the best occupation is the one that perfects judgement: cultivating my reason and seeking truth.

meta.note: Third, independent support for the choice of occupation.

arguments.justification: The chief ground of my satisfaction with the method is the assurance of exercising my reason in all matters as well as I am able, and the habit of clearer and more distinct conceptions it forms in my mind; that is why, from the time I began to apply it, it has been a source of satisfaction so intense that I believe none more perfect or more innocent can be enjoyed in this life.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. II.13 gives the ground of the satisfaction that III.5 reports.

arguments.justification: Having resolved to sweep away my opinions, and now furnished with the provisional maxims that the rebuilding required, kept in reserve with the truths of faith, I may freely proceed to rid myself of the rest of my opinions.
Being free to examine my opinions, and hoping to do it better among people than in seclusion, I resumed travelling and roamed for nine years as a spectator of the world.
Set free to rid myself of my opinions, I made it my business in each matter to look for what could fairly be doubted and prove a source of error.
By reflecting in each matter on what might be doubted and prove a source of error, I gradually rooted out all the errors that had crept into my mind.
The sceptics doubt for the sake of doubting and seek nothing but uncertainty; my doubt sought assurance, rock beneath the sand; so my doubting everything was not imitating them.
Seeking assurance, and admitting as true only what I clearly know, I tested each opinion by clear and certain reasoning rather than by feeble conjecture.

meta.note: Links the practice of doubt in III.6 to the first precept of the method.

arguments.justification: When falsehood or uncertainty is established by clear and certain reasoning, even the most doubtful matter yields at least one certain conclusion, namely that it contains nothing certain.
As the ruins of a demolished house go into the new building, so in rooting out my ill-founded opinions I gathered observations and experience that I used in establishing more certain ones.

Travelling as a spectator, uprooting my errors, keeping their ruins as material and exercising my method throughout, I progressed further in truth than books or the company of scholars would have permitted, since reasoning about real affairs holds more truth than speculation.

I had resolved never once to fail in observing my precepts, and to prepare for philosophy by continually exercising myself in my method; so throughout these years I continued to conduct my thoughts by its rules and set aside hours for mathematical problems and for questions of other sciences made almost mathematical.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. III.6 reports the practice; II.6 and II.13 are the resolutions it carries out.

arguments.justification: Since many men of the highest genius had attempted to found a more certain philosophy without success, the work must be one of very great difficulty.

I had resolved not to approach the principles of philosophy until I was more mature, and the failure of the greatest minds showed the inquiry to be of very great difficulty; so nine years passed without a determinate judgement on the disputes of the learned or a start on seeking firmer principles, and I might have waited longer still.
People credited me with a philosophy already completed; being unwilling to be thought other than I am, I had to make myself worthy of that reputation by every means.
To make myself worthy of my reputation I needed freedom from interruption; this country offers peace, solitude and the conveniences of a city all at once; so eight years ago I removed here.

In practice one must sometimes treat highly uncertain opinions as if beyond doubt, as my second maxim prescribes; but since I now wanted to attend solely to the search for truth, exactly the opposite procedure was called for. My first precept admits only what is beyond doubt, and I had long reckoned the merely probable as well-nigh false; so I resolved to reject as absolutely false everything in which I could imagine the least ground for doubt, in order to see whether anything wholly indubitable remained in my belief.
Since the senses sometimes deceive us, whatever they present admits of doubt, and my resolve requires me to suppose that nothing exists as they present it.

Some men fall into paralogisms even on the simplest matters of geometry, and I am as liable to error as anyone; so every reasoning I had taken for a demonstration admits of doubt and, by my resolve, must be rejected as false.

The very same thoughts we have awake can occur in sleep, when none of them is true; so nothing distinguishes my waking presentations from the illusions of dreams, and by my resolve I suppose they have no more truth.
From the very circumstance that I thought to doubt of the truth of other things, it is evident that I am thinking; doubting is itself a mode of thought.
While I wished to think that everything was false, it was absolutely necessary that I, who was thinking this, should be something; in order to think one must exist; therefore I exist.

Even under the most extravagant suppositions, that the senses present nothing real, that my former demonstrations are false, that my waking thoughts are no truer than dreams, the supposing is itself thinking and thinking requires existing; so no ground of doubt the sceptics can allege is capable of shaking this truth.

meta.note: The three doubt-suppositions are consumed here as the test the cogito passes.

arguments.justification: I had resolved to accept only what is wholly indubitable; 'I think, therefore I am' is the one truth that no doubt can shake; so I may without scruple take it as the first principle of the philosophy I seek.

The principles of philosophy had to be established before anything else; my provisional code left me free to rid myself of my remaining opinions; and my doubting had never sought anything but ground for assurance. So in these first meditations I gave my attention solely to the search for truth, to find whether anything in my belief was wholly indubitable.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.1 states the aim; II.13 and III.6 supply the resolutions it carries out.

arguments.justification: I have never thought my mind more perfect than the common run, and other men fall into paralogisms even on the simplest matters of geometry; so I am as open to error as any of them.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. IV.1 says 'convinced that I was as open to error as any other'; I.2 is where that modest estimate of his own mind is stated.

arguments.justification: I can suppose I have no body and that there is no world or place in which I am, yet I cannot suppose that I am not; from my doubting it follows that I am; whereas had I merely ceased to think I would have had no reason to believe I existed even if everything else were real. So thinking alone is my essence, and my existence needs no place and depends on no material thing.

Since my whole nature is to think, and that nature needs no place and depends on nothing material, the 'I', the mind by which I am what I am, is wholly distinct from the body and would remain all that it is even if the body did not exist.
My own existence as a thinking thing is beyond every doubt, while the existence of my body can still be supposed away; so the mind is more easily known than the body.

Having found one proposition I know to be true, I sought what makes it certain; in 'I think, therefore I am' nothing assures me of its truth except that I see very clearly that to think one must exist. So I may take as a general rule that whatever we conceive very clearly and distinctly is true.
I doubt, and it is a greater perfection to know than to doubt; so my being is not wholly perfect.

I asked whence I had learned to think of something more perfect than myself. My ideas of the sky, the earth, light, heat and the like contain nothing superior to me, so they could come from my own nature, or from its imperfection if they are false; but this could not be the case with the idea of a nature more perfect than mine. I could not have received it from nothing, which is manifestly impossible; nor from myself, since it is no less repugnant that the more perfect should be an effect of the less perfect than that something should come from nothing. It remained that it was placed in me by a nature really more perfect than mine, possessing every perfection of which I can form an idea; in a word, God.
Having the idea of a being more perfect than myself while my own being is not wholly perfect, I know of perfections that I do not possess.

Since I know perfections I do not possess, I am not the only being. Had I existed alone and independently, having from myself the little perfection I possess, I could for the same reason have given myself all the perfection I lack and become infinite, eternal, immutable, omniscient and all-powerful. I have not; so there is necessarily some other, more perfect Being on whom I depend and from whom I have received all that I possess.

meta.note: Second, independent argument for God's existence.

arguments.justification: To know the nature of God, whose existence the preceding reasonings established, as far as my own nature permits, I had only to consider, for every property of which I find some idea in my mind, whether possessing it is a mark of perfection; and I was assured that none which indicates imperfection is in him and that none of the rest is lacking.
Doubt, inconstancy, sadness and the like are things I would be happy to be free of, so they mark imperfection; and no imperfection is in God.

I could not deny that the ideas of sensible and corporeal things were really in my thoughts, which raised the question whether God might be corporeal as well as intelligent. But I had already clearly recognised that the intelligent nature is distinct from the corporeal; all composition is evidence of dependency, and dependency is manifestly imperfection; so it could not be a perfection in God to be compounded of these two natures, and consequently he is not so compounded.

Whatever is not wholly perfect is dependent, as I found in my own case, and that on which it depends is the wholly perfect Being; so if there are bodies, intelligences or other natures that are not wholly perfect, their existence depends on God's power such that they could not subsist without him for a single moment.

meta.note: Descartes gives this with a bare 'but that'; the step uses imperfection-implies-dependency, the converse of the stated axiom.

arguments.justification: Going over some of the geometers' simplest demonstrations about extended, divisible, movable space, I observed that the great certainty accorded to them by common consent rests solely on their being clearly conceived in accordance with the rule I had laid down.

Nothing in a geometrical demonstration assures me that its object exists: I perceive that a triangle's angles equal two right angles without perceiving that any triangle exists. But returning to the idea of a Perfect Being, I found that existence is comprised in it just as that equality is comprised in the idea of a triangle, or the equidistance of all points from the centre in the idea of a sphere, or even more clearly; and since geometrical demonstrations are certain because clearly conceived, it is at least as certain that God, this Perfect Being, exists as any demonstration of geometry can be.

meta.note: Third argument for God's existence. Together with divine-guarantee this closes the Cartesian circle: the criterion supports God's existence and God's existence supports the criterion.

arguments.justification: The certainty of geometry rests solely on its demonstrations being clearly conceived, and that rule is itself certain only because God exists and is no deceiver; so the certainty of geometry, and of all other knowledge, depends on God.

Those who never raise their thoughts above sensible objects consider everything by way of imagination, a mode of thinking limited to material things; but God and the soul are not material and their ideas were never in the senses; so to such people what cannot be imagined seems unintelligible, as if one tried to hear sounds or smell odours with one's eyes.

The schools hold that there is nothing in the understanding which was not previously in the senses; but the idea of God, like that of the soul, is in my understanding and has certainly never been in the senses; so the maxim is false.

We have a moral assurance that we have a body and that stars and an earth exist, so strong that doubting them seems extravagant; yet when asleep we can imagine ourselves with another body and seeing other stars and another earth when there is nothing of the kind, and dream thoughts are often no less vivid and distinct than waking ones. So no one of sound mind can deny that, for metaphysical certainty, entire assurance about these things is excluded, whereas the existence of the soul and of God has been established by reasons that survive this doubt.

Our ideas or notions, to the extent of their clearness and distinctness, are real and proceed from God, since all that we possess is derived from him; and it is no less repugnant that falsity should proceed from God than that truth should proceed from nothing; so to that extent they must be true. Where our ideas contain some falsity, it can only be in those that are confused and obscure and in that respect proceed from nothing, because we are not wholly perfect.

meta.note: Second justification of the criterion of truth; with criterion-from-cogito and ontological-argument it forms a cycle (the Cartesian circle), which the format records as a strongly connected component.

arguments.justification: Because I am not wholly perfect, some of my ideas may be false; the only thing that assures me that those which are clear and distinct are true is that what is real in them proceeds from a Perfect and Infinite Being, from whom no falsity can come. So the rule is certain only because God exists, is perfect, and is the source of all we possess; had we not known this, however clear and distinct our ideas, we should have no ground for assurance of their truth.

However long men of the highest genius study the question, any reason for holding waking thoughts true rather than dreams must rest on the rule that what we clearly and distinctly conceive is true; and that rule is certain only through God; so no reason can remove the doubt unless it presupposes God's existence.

The rule attaches truth to the clearness and distinctness of an idea, not to the state in which it occurs; so if a geometer discovered a new demonstration while asleep, his being asleep would not militate against its truth.

The most ordinary error of dreams is to represent objects as our external senses do; but we are deceived in the same way when awake, as when the jaundiced see everything yellow or distant bodies look smaller than they are; so this error is not prejudicial and rightly leads us to suspect the ideas of sense.

After the knowledge of God and of the soul has made the rule certain, the truth of waking thoughts need not be questioned because of dreams: a very distinct idea would be true even if it came in sleep, and the ordinary error of dreams merely reproduces the errors of sense, which we suffer awake as well; neither touches what reason clearly conceives.

Neither the senses nor the imagination can assure us of anything; that we see the sun clearly does not make it the size it appears, and that we can distinctly imagine a chimaera does not make one exist; only what reason clearly conceives is true. So whether awake or asleep we ought never to be persuaded of the truth of anything except on the evidence of our reason.
Reason plainly tells us that all our ideas or notions contain some truth; for otherwise it could not be that God, who is wholly perfect and veracious, should have placed them in us.

Because of our partial imperfection not all our thoughts can be true; truth is to be judged by reason, not by the liveliness of imagination; and our reasonings are never so clear or complete in sleep as when awake; so reason dictates that the thoughts possessing truth are to be found in waking experience rather than in dreams.

Holding firmly to the single principle by which I demonstrated the existence of God and of the soul, and admitting nothing that did not appear more clear and certain than the demonstrations of the geometers once had, I found means in a short time to satisfy myself on all the principal difficulties usually treated in philosophy.

God established these laws and impressed such notions of them on our minds that, after sufficient reflection, we cannot doubt them; and what is conceived so clearly and distinctly is true; therefore the laws are exactly observed in all that exists or takes place in the world.

Exhibiting the whole chain of truths would require treating many questions in dispute among the learned, with whom I do not wish to be embroiled; so it is better to mention only in general what these truths are.
With no other principle on which to found my reasonings than the infinite perfection of God, I demonstrated all the laws of nature about which there could be any room for doubt.
Because the laws are demonstrated from the infinite perfection of God alone, and that perfection is the same whatever he creates, no world he might create could fail to observe them.

By describing only what would happen in a new world I can throw the disputed subjects into the shade and express my judgement with greater freedom, without being obliged to adopt or refute the opinions of the learned.

Since purely material things could really have come to their present state from chaos by the laws alone, and their nature is far easier to conceive when they are seen coming gradually into existence, describing them in this way is the more intelligible course.

meta.note: An independent second reason for the same decision; kept as a separate argument.

arguments.justification: Given matter with only the properties everyone naturally understands, agitated into chaos and left to God's ordinary concurrence, the laws of nature require the greater part of it to dispose itself as heavens, while some parts compose an earth, some planets and comets, and others a sun and fixed stars.

From the nature of the matter that composes the sun and the stars under these laws, I expounded what the light found in them must be, how it traverses the immense spaces of the heavens in an instant, and how it is reflected from the planets and comets toward the earth.

Having described the substance, situation, motions and qualities of these heavens and stars and the nature and propagation of their light, I had said enough to show that nothing observable in the heavens or stars of our system must not, or at least may not, appear precisely alike in the world described.

Following the same laws, the parts of the earth so formed must tend toward its centre even though God gave its matter no weight; with water and air on its surface the heavens and especially the moon must cause an ebb and flow like our tides and an east-to-west current like that between the tropics; and mountains, seas, springs, rivers, metals, plants and all mixed bodies might be formed in it naturally.

Since besides the stars nothing I know of produces light except fire, I set out from the same laws all that pertains to its nature, production and support, and showed how it yields heat without light or light without heat, induces colours and other qualities, liquefies some bodies and hardens others, consumes almost all to ashes and smoke, and from ashes by its mere intensity forms glass.

Since the action by which God now sustains the world is the very action by which he created it, his having established the laws of nature and lent his concurrence to a mere chaos would suffice, in the course of time, to bring purely material things to the state we now observe; so this can be believed without discredit to the miracle of creation.

Whatever is not wholly perfect depends on God's power so completely that it could not subsist without him for a single moment; so the action by which he sustains the world from moment to moment is nothing other than the action by which he created it.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. V.2 cites the doctrine as commonly received among theologians; IV.4 supplies the metaphysical ground Descartes himself established for it.

arguments.justification: When I examined what functions could exist in such a body as consequences of this supposition, I found precisely all those that exist in us independently of any power of thinking, but none of those that depend on thought alone and belong to us as men.

The soul is the part of us distinct from the body, whose whole nature consists in thinking; so the functions that exist in us independently of thinking owe nothing to it, and in exactly these functions the animals void of reason may be said wholly to resemble us.

The distinctively human functions were absent from the body alone and appeared as soon as a rational soul was supposed created and joined to it in a particular manner; so a real man is such a body united with a rational soul.

Just as any liquid allowed to fall drop by drop into a highly heated vessel at once expands and dilates, so the heat of the heart, greater than anywhere else in the body, makes each drop of blood that enters its cavities rapidly expand and dilate.

The hollow vein and venous artery are always full and their orifices toward the heart cannot be closed while its cavities are empty, so blood necessarily flows in; being at once rarefied by the heat, the two large drops expand the whole heart, press shut the five inlet valves so no more blood comes down, and push open the six outlet valves, swelling the arterial vein and great artery; as the blood cools, the heart and arteries contract, the six valves close, the five reopen, and two more drops enter to begin again.

The motion I have explained follows from the arrangement of the parts that may be seen in the heart by the eye alone, from the heat that may be felt with the fingers, and from the nature of the blood as learned from experience, just as the motion of a clock follows from the power, situation and shape of its counterweights and wheels.

meta.note: Aimed at those who cannot distinguish true reasons from mere verisimilitudes.

arguments.justification: A moderate ligature hinders the blood already in the arm from returning toward the heart by the veins but cannot stop new blood coming forward through the arteries, which lie deeper, have firmer coats that are harder to compress, and carry blood from the heart with more force than the veins return it; since that blood escapes through the opened vein, there must be passages below the ligature through which it reaches the veins from the arteries.

The heart sends blood out into the arteries and never receives it back by that route, the arteries pass it through the small passages at their extremities into the small branches of the veins, and the veins return it to the heart; so its course amounts precisely to a perpetual circulation.

meta.note: Harvey's discovery, which Descartes accepts. Only the one-way passage of blood out of the heart is needed here, not Descartes' own rarefaction account of why the heart beats.

arguments.justification: The valves along the veins permit blood only to return from the extremities to the heart, never to pass outward from the middle of the body; so the blood in the veins must have reached the extremities by another route, the arteries, and be on its way back to the heart.

meta.note: Second, independent support attributed to Harvey.

arguments.justification: If all the blood in the body can leave in a short time through one cut artery, even one tied close to the heart and cut between the heart and the tie so that it can only have come from the heart, then all the blood in the body passes through the heart and out by the arteries.

meta.note: Third, independent support attributed to Harvey.

arguments.justification: Because the blood that leaves the heart by the arteries returns to it by the veins, the veins are never emptied by feeding the heart nor the arteries overfilled by receiving all the blood that passes through it.

The difference between the blood of the veins and that of the arteries can only arise from its being rarefied and, as it were, distilled by passing through the heart, which is why it is thinner, livelier and warmer just after leaving the heart and why the difference is marked only in the neighbourhood of the heart.

The consistency of the coats of the arterial vein and the great artery shows that the blood is impelled against them with more force than against the veins, as it would be if it were driven out of the heart by rarefaction.

Why should the left cavity and the great artery be wider than the right cavity and the arterial vein, unless the blood of the venous artery, having already passed through the heart and been in the lungs, is thinner and rarefies more readily and to a higher degree than the blood coming straight from the hollow vein?

meta.note: Descartes also cites the pulse: physicians could infer nothing from it unless blood of differing nature were rarefied to differing degrees by the heart's warmth.

arguments.justification: The blood is heated anew each time it passes through the heart and is then carried to every part of the body; that is why withdrawing blood from a part withdraws its heat, and why a heart as hot as glowing iron could not warm the hands and feet unless it continually sent them new blood.

The blood rarefied almost into vapour in the right ventricle passes to the lungs, where the fresh air brought in by breathing thickens it and converts it anew into blood before it enters the left cavity; without this it would be unfit to nourish the fire there.

Animals without lungs have only one cavity in the heart, and unborn children, who cannot use their lungs, have a hole and a tube by which the blood bypasses them; this is just what should be expected if the office of the lungs were to re-thicken blood rarefied in the right ventricle.

The heart sends heat and the more fluid parts of the blood to the stomach through the arteries to dissolve the food; the juice of food becomes blood by being distilled through the heart perhaps one or two hundred times a day; and the force with which the rarefied blood passes toward the extremities leaves some of its parts in the members, selected by the situation, shape and smallness of the pores they meet, as variously perforated sieves separate different kinds of grain.

The most agitated and penetrating parts of the blood are the fittest to compose the animal spirits, and they reach the brain simply because the arteries that carry them leave the heart in the most direct lines and, by the rules of mechanics which are those of nature, when many parts tend at once to a point without room for all, the stronger drive the weaker aside; from the brain the spirits pass through the nerves into the muscles and give motion to all the members.

Given the fabric of the nerves and muscles and the spirits that move them, changes in the brain suffice to produce waking, sleep and dreams, the ideas impressed by light, sound, odour, taste and heat and by hunger and thirst, the common sense that receives them, the memory that retains them, the fantasy that recombines them and distributes the spirits to the muscles, and movements as suited to objects as ours are apart from the will; as we see heads still move and bite the earth shortly after being struck off, though no longer animated.

Human automata perform many different movements with few pieces; the animal body, with its vast multitude of bones, muscles, nerves, arteries and veins, is likewise a machine, but made by the hands of God and therefore incomparably better arranged and capable of more admirable movements than any machine of human invention.

Everything an irrational animal does is done by the disposition of its organs; so a machine exactly resembling an ape or other irrational animal in organs and outward form would do all that the animal does, and we could have no means of knowing that it was of a different nature.

We can easily conceive a machine so made that it emits words, even words corresponding to the action of external objects on its organs, as when touched in one place it asks what we want and in another cries out that it is hurt; but arranging words variously so as to reply appositely to whatever is said in its presence, as men of the lowest intellect can, calls for the universal instrument of reason, not for any particular arrangement of organs.

Reason serves alike on every occasion, whereas organs need a particular arrangement for each particular action; so it is morally impossible for any machine to have enough different organs to act in all the occurrences of life as our reason enables us to act, and however well it does some things it will fail in others, revealing that it acts from the disposition of its organs and not from knowledge.

These two tests, the use of words or signs to declare thoughts and acting from knowledge in every occurrence of life, are most certain means of knowing that a machine bearing the image of our body and imitating our actions is not really a man.

Magpies and parrots have organs fit to utter words yet cannot speak so as to show they understand, while men born deaf and dumb, with fewer of the organs others use in speaking than the brutes have, spontaneously invent signs to declare their thoughts; so having the organs is neither sufficient nor necessary for speech, and the animals' silence is not for want of organs.

By the same two tests we may know the difference between men and brutes: there is no man so dull, not even an idiot, that he cannot join words to make his thoughts understood, and there is no animal, however perfect, that can do the like, and not for want of organs; this proves not only that the brutes have less reason than man but that they have none at all.

Very little is required to be able to speak, and animals of one species differ in capacity and teachability as men do; so if the brutes had reason of our kind, the most perfect ape or parrot of its species would at least equal the most stupid or crack-brained child in this; it does not; hence the soul of the brutes is of a nature wholly different from ours, and they have no reason at all.

The natural movements that indicate the passions can be imitated by machines as well as displayed by animals, so they are not speech; and the brutes cannot, as some of the ancients thought, speak a language we fail to understand, for with organs so like ours they could communicate their thoughts to us as easily as to their fellows, and they do not.

If the animals' superior industry in certain actions proved that they had mind, they would have more reason than any of us and would surpass us in all things; but the same animals show no industry at all in many other actions; so their skill proves rather that they are destitute of reason and that nature acts in them by the disposition of their organs, as a clock made only of wheels and weights counts the hours and measures time more exactly than we can with all our skill.

Whatever the power of matter produces acts by the disposition of its organs and needs a particular arrangement for each action; the rational soul, whose whole nature is to think and whose reason serves on every occasion, is of a wholly different kind; so it cannot be educed from the power of matter as the other things I described can.

meta.note: Descartes says only that he had shown this in the withheld treatise; the premises here are the ones Part V itself supplies (the soul as thinking thing, and the universality of reason versus the particularity of organs).

arguments.justification: Since the rational soul cannot come from the power of matter, and whatever exists either arises from matter under the laws of nature or is expressly created by God, it must be expressly created.

A soul lodged in the human body only as a pilot in a ship might move its members but could not have sensations and appetites like ours; since we have them, the soul must be joined and united more closely to the body, and so constitutes a real man.

If our soul were of the same nature as that of the brutes, we would have nothing to hope for or fear after this life more than flies and ants; such a belief leads feeble minds astray from virtue; so, after the error of denying God, which I have already refuted, no error is more powerful in leading them from the straight path.

When we know how far the soul of the brutes differs from ours, we comprehend much better the reasons which establish that our soul, a thinking thing not derivable from the power of matter, is of a nature wholly independent of the body.

meta.note: The comparison with the brutes is offered as an aid to comprehending the reasons rather than as a strict premise; it is included because Descartes makes it part of his case.

arguments.justification: What is wholly independent of the body in its nature is not destroyed when the body is, and I had already found that the mind would continue to be all that it is even if the body did not exist; consequently the soul is not liable to die with it.
The soul is not liable to die with the body, and no other causes are observed capable of destroying it; so we are naturally led to judge that it is immortal.

If persons whose authority over my actions I rank almost with my own reason have condemned a doctrine in which my careful judgement found nothing prejudicial to religion or the state, then my judgement of my own doctrines, formed with the same care, may be just as mistaken.

meta.note: care-in-belief-and-expression is conceded here rather than used: the fear arises notwithstanding his care.

arguments.justification: Fearing that some of my doctrines may have departed from the truth, and being unwilling to publish anything that might prove false or hurtful, I altered my purpose of publishing the treatise.

Not to accept anything as true without clearly knowing it to be so, and not to publish what may be false or hurtful, are the rules I follow; hence the great care I have always taken not to believe new opinions without the most certain demonstrations, and not to express anything that might harm anyone.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. VI.1 reports the care; II.7 and the implicit VI.1 rule are what it consists in.

arguments.justification: In what regards conduct everyone is full of his own wisdom, and only rulers and prophets are entitled to mend the manners of others; others had speculations that pleased them as mine pleased me; so nothing bound me to publish while my results were only speculative or served only to regulate my own actions.

Having seen how far my notions of physics carry us and how they differ from what has been taught, I perceived that they make possible a practical philosophy: knowing the surrounding bodies as artisans know their crafts, we could apply them to every use and become masters and possessors of nature.

Mastery of nature would yield an infinity of arts by which we could enjoy the fruits of the earth without trouble, and, above all, the preservation of health, which is the first of all the goods of this life.

Since the mind depends so intimately on the condition of the bodily organs, any means of making men wiser and more ingenious must be a means of improving the body, that is, must be sought in medicine.

Principles that make possible so great a benefit to human life cannot be kept concealed without sinning grievously against the law that binds us to promote, as far as in us lies, the general good of mankind.

I had already chosen to devote my whole life to cultivating my reason and seeking truth. Health is the chief good and even wisdom depends on it; what medicine now knows is almost nothing beside what could free us from countless maladies if we knew their causes and remedies; so the science of nature that would ground medicine is the most necessary of all, and I resolve to spend the rest of my life in seeking it.

The only things that can stop one who follows my path are the shortness of life and the want of experiments; both are overcome if many contribute experiments and each begins where the last left off; so faithfully publishing what I have found and inciting others is the most effectual provision against them.

Since I mean to spend my whole life on this science, and publishing is the best provision against the two impediments to completing it, I ought to communicate all I have found and incite men of superior genius to go farther.

The laws of nature and the chain of truths I deduced from them resolved the principal difficulties of philosophy and explained the heavens, the earth, light, fire and the body of man; making trial of these general notions on particular difficulties is what showed me how far they carry us and how much they differ from the principles employed until now.

meta.note: Reconstructed link between the summary of the physics in Part V and the estimate of it in VI.2.

arguments.justification: The soul is united to the body closely enough to have sensations and appetites, and waking, sleep, dreams, the impressions of the senses, memory and fantasy all arise from changes in the brain and the motion of the spirits; so the mind is intimately dependent on the condition and arrangement of the organs of the body.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. VI.2 asserts the dependence; V.7 and V.8 are where Descartes describes the mechanism that makes it plausible to him.

arguments.justification: Because rare phenomena only mislead so long as the causes of the ordinary ones are unknown, and their conditions are too minute to detect, one should begin with what the senses present spontaneously and cannot be ignorant of.

The first causes and the commonest effects are found by reason alone from innate truths, but on descending to particular bodies one can no longer proceed without many experiments; so their necessity grows the further one advances.

My principles explain every effect I have observed, but usually in several possible ways; only an experiment whose outcome would differ between those ways can show on which the effect actually depends.
Since further knowledge of particulars needs experiments that far exceed my own hands and income, my progress in the knowledge of nature will be greater or less according to my means of making them.

My progress depends on experiments I cannot make alone; a treatise showing the public advantage would induce all who truly have the common good at heart to share their experiments and assist with the rest; so I should make my findings known.

meta.note: His original hope for the withheld treatise; a second route to the same conclusion, independent of the duty argument.

arguments.justification: Writing as if for readers makes me examine my results more thoroughly; it loses no opportunity of serving the public as far as in me lies; and after my death the writings can be put to use by whoever receives them.
As the rich acquire more easily and victorious commanders grow stronger, so with sound principles won by a few victories I do not despair of attaining far more than the little I now know.

Expecting, with two or three more victories and the years nature ordinarily allows, to attain far more than I yet know, my expectation of employing my time aright is great, and so I am the more bound to husband it.

Though evident, my principles cannot accord with all the diverse opinions of others, so publishing them would surely awaken opposition, and answering it would frequently turn me aside from my grand design.

Though everyone is bound to be useful to others, it is good to forgo a present profit for a much greater advantage to posterity; publishing now would cost the time I must husband to finish my work; so I will not consent to publication in my lifetime.

Taken together: publishing would rob me of time; the objections it provoked would not profit me; others could gain little from my unfinished thoughts; and it would bring me no assistance I could accept. Hence for three years I have been unwilling to publish the treatise, and I resolved to publish no work so general in my lifetime.

meta.note: VI.8 says these considerations 'taken together' were the reason.

arguments.justification: Though I know my liability to error, experience shows that objections rarely raise what I had not already considered and that no critic has proved more rigorous than I; and the disputations of the schools have never produced a new truth; so the opposition publishing would provoke could not profit me.

meta.note: Answers the objection that opposition would reveal errors and enlist helpers; i-am-liable-to-error is conceded but not a premise.

arguments.justification: Even acute hearers so alter my opinions in repeating them that I cannot recognise them, and scarcely any disciple has surpassed his master; which shows that what is learned from another is never seized and made one's own as what one has discovered oneself.
Since no one masters a thing so well from another as from having discovered it himself, whatever superior minds exist, none could carry my thoughts through so well as I who began them.

My thoughts are not yet far enough advanced to be applied to practice, and if anyone can carry them that far it is I rather than another; so others could not derive much advantage from having them communicated.
Since even those who hear my opinions directly misreport them, posterity should credit nothing as mine that I have not published myself.

Because their obscurity is what lets them defend anything, and my principles are the simplest and most evident, publishing mine would be like throwing open the windows on their dark cave; hence such persons have an interest in my silence.

Had I been taught all my truths without labour I would have known nothing beyond them and never acquired my facility for finding new ones; so the habit of seeking in order is worth more than any instruction.

Those able to go further than I can rediscover for themselves what I have found, since what remains is harder; and the habit they acquire by seeking in order will benefit them more than my instructions; so this discourse gives them all they need.

If superior men seek a reputation for learning, verisimilitude serves them better than my principles; if they prefer the knowledge of a few truths, this discourse already gives them all they need to find them for themselves.
Neither the philosophers of the schools, who have an interest in my silence, nor superior men, who can find the truth better by themselves, would gain by my publishing my principles.

meta.note: A second, independent argument for the same conclusion as others-gain-little.

arguments.justification: Volunteers promise more than they perform and expect repayment in time-wasting talk, whereas paid artisans are stimulated to accuracy by the hope of gain; so the latter are the only hands worth employing besides one's own.

One man cannot make all the experiments, yet the only usable hands are paid ones and the experiments others have made cannot be relied on; so even for a man known capable of the greatest discoveries, all others could do is pay for his experiments and leave him undisturbed.

The only useful help would be money and undisturbed leisure; but I neither promise enough to deserve it nor imagine the public interested, and I would not accept a favour of which I might be thought unworthy; so publishing could bring me no help I could use.

meta.note: The conclusion is implicit in VI.7 and counted in VI.8 among the considerations taken together.

arguments.justification: Having neither courted fame nor hidden my doings as if they were crimes, and yet having unavoidably acquired some reputation, I am bound at least to keep that reputation from being bad.

If I published nothing, those who knew my earlier intention might think my reasons less creditable than they are; I am bound not to be ill spoken of; and I can choose specimens that expose neither my principles nor myself to much controversy; so I publish this account with some specimens.

My design is daily delayed for want of experiments I cannot make alone, and I owe it to myself not to let posterity reproach me for never telling them how they could have helped; specimens that avoid controversy let me do this; so I publish them with an account of my designs.

meta.note: Second, independent reason for publishing the Discourse and essays.

arguments.justification: I owe the public what little I have found, and I set out to describe the path I have followed so that each may judge it; yet the physics itself must stay unpublished in my lifetime. Specimens that expose neither my principles nor myself to much controversy, joined to an account of my doings and designs, discharge the one obligation without breaching the other.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. It makes explicit that the decision to publish reconciles the duty of VI.2 with the withholding of VI.4-8; VI.8 gives two further reasons, recorded as separate arguments.

arguments.justification: If objections are sent to my publisher I can append my reply, and readers seeing both at once will more easily determine where the truth lies.

Although the causes demonstrate the effects and the effects the causes, experience already makes most of the effects certain; the causes serve to explain them rather than to establish them, while the reality of the causes is established by the reality of the effects; so there is no circle.

Though I believe I can deduce these hypotheses from my first truths, doing so would give hasty minds occasion to build extravagant philosophies on what they took to be my principles and have me blamed for it; so I refrain.

My first precept forbids accepting anything as true that I do not clearly know to be so, and reason alone, not the senses, the imagination, or the opinions of others, is to be the ground of persuasion; so the opinions that are truly mine were adopted neither because others held them nor because they did not, but solely because reason convinced me of their truth.

meta.note: Reconstructed link. VI.10 describes the practice; II.7 and IV.8 are the rules it follows.

arguments.justification: Since making and adjusting the machines requires skill and practice, failure at the first attempt no more condemns the invention than a beginner's failure to play a piece condemns the sheet music.

Good sense is equal in all men and opinions differ only through the way we conduct our thoughts; my own opinions, if their reasons are weighed, are simple and conformed to common sense; so a reader who uses unprejudiced natural reason is as fit a judge of them as any, and a better one than someone who defers only to the ancients.

meta.note: The link to Part I is implicit; VI.11 simply states the expectation.

arguments.justification: I describe my path so that each reader may judge it for himself; I expect those who use unprejudiced natural reason to judge my opinions better than those who heed only the ancients, and French reaches them; while those who join good sense to study, whom alone I want as judges, will not refuse my reasoning for being in the vulgar tongue.

My inclination is so opposed to every other pursuit, above all those that help some only by harming others, that I could not succeed in any of them; so I give my remaining time to this one occupation.

meta.note: A supporting consideration offered alongside the public declaration, not the main argument.

arguments.justification: My progress depends on experiments that exceed my own means, so I cannot be certain what I shall accomplish; and I hold it a sin against good sense to bind myself by a promise about the future; so I bind myself to the public by no promise about my future progress.
